content: The bow is near the bridge. The sound is glassy and has much noise
The bow is above the fingerboard. The sound is softer
The wood of the bow hits the string (battuto) or moves across it (tratto)
The string hits the fingerboard. Also called Bartók pizzicato
The player strums a chord across the strings
example: Bartók, Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta IV

content: Natural harmonics (a light touch on an open string) and artificial harmonics (one firm finger and one light finger)
A slide of the light finger gives a chain of harmonics ("seagull" effect)
The bow is between the bridge and the tailpiece. The pitch is high and not exact
The same note on an open string and then on stopped strings, in more and more players. The sound becomes harder
Two string orchestras on the two sides of the stage answer each other
example: Bartók, Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta II and IV

content: The player rolls the tongue. The sound goes from a soft cooing to a growl. It needs more air than a normal note. Notation: tremolo strokes and a word (flz., frull.)
example: Tchaikovsky, The Nutcracker (flutes). Corigliano, Pied Piper Fantasy (a high, shrill flutter-tongued note of the soloist)

content: The player hits the keys with no air. A soft percussion sound at the pitch of the fingering
Two or more notes at the same time, from special fingerings
Air through the instrument with no tone, or with a small part of the tone
The player moves the pitch with the lips or the fingers
The player blows the reed in a special way to get a raw sound
example: Corigliano, Oboe Concerto (1975): the sound of the North African rhaita

technique: A second instrument of the same player
content: The soloist changes to a tin whistle for the march
As on woodwinds. On horns it can sound like animals
example: Strauss, Don Quixote, variation 2 (horns: the sheep)

technique: Mutes and objects in the bell
content: Each mute type gives a different colour
example: Bartók, Concerto for Orchestra II (muted trumpets in major seconds)

content: Trombones slide between notes
example: Bartók, Concerto for Orchestra IV (trombones and woodwinds interrupt the theme). Corigliano, Clarinet Concerto I ("glissandi of jagged canons")

technique: Half valve, pitch bend, double buzz
content: Sounds between the notes and sounds with noise
Five horns behind the stage, two trumpets at the rear of the hall, two clarinets high at the sides. The music for them "specifically shouldn't be synchronized"
A bow on the edge of a vibraphone bar, a cymbal, or a gong. A long note with no attack
The player moves the pedal while the drum sounds
example: Bartók, Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta III. Concerto for Orchestra IV: 10 pitches in about 20 seconds

content: The cymbal sounds through the drum. The pedal changes the colour
The player lowers a gong into water after the stroke. The pitch slides
A side drum alone starts and ends the movement
The player plucks the strings, hits them with a mallet, or slides a finger along a string
The player holds keys down with no sound. The open strings ring when other notes sound
The palm or the arm plays all keys of an area
The piano is a member of the percussion group. The celesta player also plays the piano with four hands
example: Bartók, Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta

content: A light touch at the middle of the string. The note is one octave higher and has a bell sound
The player plucks the string at its low end. The sound is dry, as a guitar
A soft tremolo of the two hands on some notes: a whisper
A change of the pedal while the string sounds moves the pitch by a semitone. A glissando across the strings gives the scale of the pedal setting
